lesson.title: Integrating a Flat Rate: The Constant Rule
lesson.summary: The constant rule states that ∫k dx = kx + C for any constant k, because a straight line with slope k is exactly what differentiates back to that constant rate.
lesson.body:
Some integrands are as simple as possible: a plain number with no variable attached at all, such as ∫7 dx. It might not be obvious at first what function has a constant derivative, since every rule you have used so far involved a variable raised to some power. The constant rule fills this gap directly.

The rule states: ∫k dx = kx + C, for any constant k. The reasoning is short and direct. We need a function whose derivative equals the constant k everywhere. A straight line of the form kx has slope k at every point, and the derivative of a linear function y = kx is simply its slope, so d/dx[kx] = k. That is exactly the integrand we started with, which confirms the rule.

Worked example: ∫7 dx. Here k = 7, so the rule gives 7x + C directly. Check by differentiating: d/dx[7x] = 7, which matches the integrand exactly, and the constant of integration is included since infinitely many lines of the form 7x + C all share that same constant slope of 7.

It is also worth noticing that the constant rule is really just a special case of the power rule for integration, using the fact that any constant k can be written as k · x^0, since x^0 = 1. Applying the power rule to x^0 gives x^1/1 = x, so k · x^0 integrates to k · x = kx, matching the constant rule exactly. Seeing this connection is a useful check: you do not need to memorize the constant rule as an entirely separate fact, since it falls directly out of the power rule you already know, applied to the special exponent zero.
